title: Scott says its new Addict Gravel is built for adventure and has the features to prove it
content:
Cyclist
Scott says its new Addict Gravel is built for adventure and has the features to prove it 

The Scott Addict Gravel has been updated for the first time since 2020, becoming an adventure gravel bike instead of a race bike. Thanks to a very skinny driveside chainstay, the new design has an impressive 57mm tyre clearance and neatly secretes a full saddlebag’s worth of kit in various hatches around its frameset.

Comfort has been bumped up by a claimed 60% at the rear and 30% at the front, thanks to flex-inducing finishing kit and clever frame shaping at the seatstays and forks.

Organic tube transitions and structurally efficient shaping have allowed a 75g weight drop in the HMX-level frame, with builds at 8.4kg claimed to be achievable. That said, Scott says the bike is best suited to long days on rugged terrain. Geometry updates mean the bike shouldn’t be used with less than 45mm tyres.

The Scott Addict Gravel is available in seven sizes and five builds, with prices ranging from £2,499 to £7,999.

Blurring lines and shifting genres

Scott’s Addict Gravel has been in the brand’s lineup for about a decade and in that time has undergone significant development. Its roots can be traced back to the Addict CX, Scott’s cyclocross bike, in 2016. Although ultimately there are features all of Scott’s ‘Addict’ platforms still share – finishing kit standards, frame storage and lightweight design, for example – the latest revision of the Addict Gravel moves the model further away than ever from its aggressive roots.

With storage options, relaxed handling and 57mm tyre clearance, the latest Addict Gravel is built for exploring rather than racing. Not that you’d know it from the new frameset’s sleek looks, which bear more resemblance to the racy bikes Scott is known for than a rugged, go-anywhere machine. That the brand looks to have successfully balanced both good looks and utility speaks to the skill and innovation employed in the Addict Gravel’s design.

The bike’s parallel, straight chainstays are a good example – bikes with 57mm tyre clearance using a road Q-factor and 425mm stays, as the Addict Gravel does, usually have to resort to dropping the chainstays in order to make the back end of the frame stiff and tight enough.

‘We achieved normal-looking chanstays by squeezing the driveside one to just 8.5mm at its narrowest,’ says engineer Jean-Francois Boivin. ‘It was a big engineering challenge because our vendor told us the thinnest hollow tube (so the Addict Gravel can be compatible with mechanical gearing) they could manufacture to was 10.5mm. But we wanted that extra 2mm to get to 57mm, because that’s 2.2in MTB tyre territory and gives market-leading clearance.’

The solution was unorthodox: the fabricators insert a 5mm thick Teflon plate into the chainstay tube at the moment of pre-forming (laying the carbon in the mould). The plate stays solid during the composite curing and doesn’t stick to it, so can be removed after the chainstay is made, but offers the support during manufacturing for the tube to be formed.

Makeover at the front

With the back end made tidy, the front has received a similar spruce up. As it has done in other Addict platforms, Scott has moved to a skinnier steerer to allow both a narrow head tube and integrated cables, which is paired with a new cockpit from Syncros (though as the steerer is still round, expander shim can be used to fit conventional stems).

‘With Syncros being our components brand, we have similar cockpits on our other Addict bikes but didn’t just carry one over,’ says Max Koenen, Scott’s head of road bike engineering. ‘In the Addict Gravel’s one we tweaked the ergonomics for gravel. Increased forward sweep on the tops improves wrist clearance but the reach has been shortened to make swapping form the tops to the hoods easier. The drops also position the shifters neutrally, rather than making then angling them outward, despite having flare, because we’ve started the flare lower down.’

The bars’ tricks don’t end there. Their bar ends discretely house both a small multitool and a tubeless plug kit.

‘Mechanicals are a fact of life on an adventure so internal storage is essential on bikes like the Addict Gravel,’ says Boivin. ‘We wanted the bike to have benchmark practicality, but it had to be all but invisible.’

As a result you’ll notice, or perhaps fail to, that all frame mounting options – of which there are several – use countersunk bolts so as not to disrupt the frameset’s clean lines. The fork mounts are hidden further, having been placed on the inside of the blades.

‘Using a band-on mount, we found if the mounts were installed on the inside of the blades we could position the cages to the rear of the fork as opposed to on each outside face,’ says Boivin. ‘This puts the mass the mounts carry closer to the steering axis, reducing its inertia so it affects handling less.’

Hidden extras

There’s also a full ‘Save the Day’ kit housed in a hatch on the down tube just in front of the bottom bracket.

‘We’ve put our storage hatch here because the tools it contains – inner tube, tyre levers and mini-pump – are for when the rider’s in trouble rather that stuff they’ll need often. For that gear Syncros has made a custom frame bag,’ says Boivin. ‘FEA structural analysis determined that in front of the BB was a better location for the hatch than the more common option of under the down tube bottle cage.’

Boivin explains Scott was required to add 25g of material to recoup the stiffness loss of including the opening under the BB.

‘On the down tube we would have needed to add 55g of reinforcement,’ he says. ‘Plus the hatch door can be just 12g located where it is. If it was under a bottle cage, it would need to be sturdier to support the bottle, and would easily have to be over 50g.’

It’s features like these that help Scott keep the Addict Gravel, though it’s focus has shifted, true to its more aggressive heritage in areas such as weight.

Scott will offer the bike in to carbon blends. A medium frame in the HMX blend weighs a claimed 794g, with the lower tier HMF blend weighing 990g. They save 75g and 25g respectively compared to the last generation bike.

‘The shaping of the frameset is structurally efficient rather than aero, mostly,’ says Boivin. ‘Tube junctions are organic – the smooth transitions are “fibre-friendly” meaning we can use minimal material to shape them. With us using of polypropylene mandrels in several areas of the frame – we’re the only ones to do it in the fork as well – during the fabrication process, we can squeeze out excess resin and ensure carbon swatches stay where they’re placed, meaning we don’t need to include redundant material as insurance. This allows such a light frameset weight.’

Balancing flex and rigidity

While Scott would almost always seek to minimise weight, stiffness is another matter because off-road, a harsh frameset can be very detrimental to performance.

‘We looked to our mountain bike designs here,’ says Koenen. ‘Too much stiffness means the bike lacks control and traction, so we made the Addict Gravel in four lay-ups to determine the right blend.’

Scott settled on a make-up where stiffness at the BB and head tube junctions is 5% lower than before. That said, the bike is rated beyond typical drop-bar impact standards to the more rigorous MTB ones, but clever shaping ensures while tough, the bike should offer a cosseting ride experience.

‘Both the seatstays and fork legs are pre-bowed outward,’ says Koenen. ‘When bumps are transmitted into the frame, these bows visibly flex to absorb them. With the syncros seatpost and cockpit also designed to flex vertically, this means versus the previous generation Addict Gravel, the new one is 60% comfier at the rear and 30% at the front.’

Substantial fit and handling changes

Making the Addict Gravel from something quite racy to more of an explorer and bumping its tyre clearance so significantly also require a fair bit of geometrical adjustment.

‘We made a test mule with adjustable headset cups to change head tube angle by +/-2°, pairing that with a fork that had an adjustable rake as well so we could test lots of geometries. We have an indoor test track at Scott HQ and as we’re all riders, we encouraged our colleagues to test setups out and feed their experience back to determine the best solution.

‘Stack is 10mm higher, but the bottom bracket is lower so the bigger tyres don’t affect balance,’ says Boivin. ‘Reach is also 10mm longer. The cockpit it 10mm shorter to compensate in terms of ride position, but this extra front centre length increases the stability. To preserve agility at lower speed though, we’ve increased the fork rake so the trail didn’t get too long.’

The Addict Gravel will be offered in seven sizes and five builds, detailed below.
